source.title: Limited Gradient Descent: Learning With Noisy Labels
source.authors: Yi Sun; Yan Tian; Yi-Ping Xu; Jianxiang Li

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether networks learn regular and noisy label patterns in a particular order and measures test accuracy across label-noise levels, using LGD and early-stopping comparisons rather than the original random-label fitting procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2016) and Arpit et al. (2017) for prior findings; those cited results are not rows. Its own MNIST pattern experiments and CIFAR-100 noise-level results are included. CIFAR-10 noise-sweep results appear only in figures and are not numerically reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures learning order for clean, systematically mislabeled, and randomly mislabeled subsets in seven datasets, bearing on V6. Its LGD performance comparisons do not establish random-label interpolation or V4's joint training-fit and test-error trajectory.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that learning prioritizes large regular patterns over smaller conflicting regular patterns and chaotic patterns, and use this ordering to motivate LGD checkpoint selection without clean validation data. They report comparable CIFAR performance and improved Clothing-1M performance relative to corresponding validation-based methods.
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces LGD, which creates reverse-label samples and chooses a stopping point from leftover-to-reverse training accuracy. Experiments use noisy-label settings rather than full random relabeling of the training set.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with dataset, noise type and fraction, loss method, and whether LGD is used. The paper reports sensitivity to validation-set size in CIFAR-10 figures.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 6 compares validation-based checkpoint selection with LGD across noise levels. Symmetric-noise test accuracy decreases with corruption, but neither method's selected score establishes perfect training fit or the full corruption trajectory.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LGD can select checkpoints with test accuracy broadly comparable to clean-validation selection under the tested CIFAR-100 noise conditions.

record.problems: The cited claim about memorization is not directly reproduced with fully random labels. The noise sweeps stop below complete corruption; training-set fit at each noise level is not reported. CIFAR-10 sweep values and the pattern-learning curves are figure-only.
record.rows_left_out: CIFAR-10 experiments in Figure 4 and Figure 5 show results only in figures; no numerical values reconstructed. Clothing-1M Table 7 reports comparisons for noisy real-world labels, but does not measure a version-specific random-label or noise-sweep result and is omitted.

untested.parts: Complete random relabeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Time to fit random versus true labels and convergence time as corruption increases. Subset learning order does not measure these comparisons.

Perfect training fit across corruption fractions jointly with steadily worsening test error through complete random labeling. Table 6 reports selected early-stopping performance rather than this trajectory.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it alone causes poor true-label generalization.

Learning order outside the tested pattern proportions, including when a conflicting systematic noise pattern exceeds the clean pattern in size; comparison of wholly clean and wholly random-label training runs.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Artificial label corruption supplies the training task; the learning order itself is measured rather than explicitly instructed or rewarded. Figures 2–3 are supported by explicit prose, although numerical curves cannot be recovered from the supplied text. Figures 4–5 are already declared in rows_left_out. The conditional LGD theorems do not independently demonstrate failure of V6 outside the tested proportions.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment uses a completely random labeling of the full training set or reports zero or near-zero training error with test error at chance.
No comparison of training time for fitting random versus true labels, or convergence time across fractions of corrupted labels.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.

The study evaluates test accuracy across several label-noise fractions, but does not test the full range from no corruption to complete random labeling or establish perfect training-set fit at each fraction.

Dropout and Mixup are used in noisy-label experiments, but the study does not test whether regularization prevents fitting completely random labels or whether removing it alone harms generalization on true labels.
The experiments compare large-scale clean patterns with small-scale regular or chaotic patterns; they do not compare real labels against a completely random labeling of the same training set.
